case_info.scenario: A 75-year-old man with myelodysplastic syndrome (MDS) with isolated deletion 5q (del5q) presented with multiple nonhealing skin ulcers on the chest and upper extremities. Four years earlier, he started taking lenalidomide, 10 mg/d (28-day cycle), to treat worsening anemia; after 2 cycles of treatment, he became transfusion independent. Since then, he has remained stable with the same dose and schedule of lenalidomide without significant adverse effects. The presenting skin lesions developed 1 month before presentation and began as small pustules that rapidly transformed into painful ulcers. He was treated with valacyclovir for a presumed diagnosis of shingles, but the lesions did not improve. Because of suspected necrotizing fasciitis, he underwent incision and drainage of the lesions. Cultures from the surgical specimen grew methicillin-resistantStaphylococcus hemolyticus. However, the lesions continued to worsen despite vancomycin and additional debridement. Thus, he was transferred to our facility. Physical examination showed multiple cutaneous ulcers with gray undermined borders and red papules of varying depths involving the chest, back, and upper extremity; lesions were as large as 9 × 15 cm. A complete blood cell count showed a white blood cell count of 16.2 × 103/μL (to convert to 109/L, multiply by 1.0) with an absolute neutrophil count of 12.7 × 103/μL, hemoglobin level of 9.4 g/dL (to convert to g/L, multiply by 10.0), and platelet count of 262 × 103/μL with no circulating blasts. Results of additional laboratory studies, including blood culture and tests for herpes zoster virus (via polymerase chain reaction), antinuclear antibody, rheumatoid factor, and antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibody were all negative. Additionally, the patient also had hypertension and hypercholesterolemia for which he was taking lisinopril and simvastatin, respectively. Pathologic sampling from skin lesions demonstrated a dense dermal infiltrate with predominantly neutrophils along with reactive histiocytes, fibroblasts, and angioplasia (Figure, A). Immunohistochemical staining showed myeloperoxidase-positive neutrophils (Figure, B), histiocytic markers (CD43, CD63, CD168), and CD117-positive mast cells, but no immature myeloid precursors. Results of Grocott-Gomori methenamine silver staining were unremarkable.
case_info.caption: A, Hematoxylin-eosin staining shows polymorphonuclear neutrophils admixed with scattered histiocytes and vasculatures with a prominent endothelial lining. B, Immunohistochemical staining shows myeloperoxidase-positive neutrophils peripherally and in aggregates.
case_info.explanation: Pyoderma gangrenosum (PG) is a rare neutrophilic dermatosis (ND) characterized by painful erythematous or inflammatory papules that often progress to ulcers with a violaceous border.1A large cohort study showed that PG is commonly associated with other systemic disorders, such as inflammatory bowel disease (41% of participants), inflammatory arthropathies (21%), hematological malignancies (11%), and solid tumors (7%),2with an overall incidence of 0.63 per 100 000 person-years.3It frequently occurs in young or middle-aged adults (median age, 51.6 years) and it is more common in women.2 Cutaneous lesions in PG mimic lesions of other skin disorders, and no finding is pathognomonic for PG. Therefore, diagnosis of PG depends largely on clinical history, histological findings, and exclusion of other inflammatory or ulcerative cutaneous diseases.1,2While early-stage PG shows intradermal neutrophils and perifollicular inflammation, ulcerative PG at later stages typically demonstrates epidermal or dermal necrosis, infiltration of inflammatory cells, and abscess formation.1Deposition of IgM, C3, and fibrin can be observed in PG, but these findings are nonspecific.4There are 4 morphologic subtypes of PG. Ulcerative PG is characterized by rapid progression of inflammatory papules, pustules, or vesicles to ulcerative lesions. Bullous PG is characterized by rapid development of inflammatory bullae. Pustular PG commonly occurs in patients with inflammatory bowel disease during an acute exacerbation. Vegetative PG is characterized by localized and superficial lesions with an indolent disease course.1 The pathogenesis of PG depends primarily on immune dysregulation and genetic factors. Previous studies have shown that gene expression levels of proinflammatory cytokines (eg, tumor necrosis factor α and interleukins [ILs] IL-1α, IL-1β, IL-8, IL-12, IL-15, IL-17, IL-23, and IL-36) and levels of pattern recognition receptors are increased in the cutaneous lesions of PG, leading to activation of inflammasomes and dysregulation of innate and adaptive immunities.1Furthermore, several reports from familial cases of PG suggest that genetic factors can play important roles in PG pathogenesis,5and variants inPTSTPIP1/CD2BP1, MEFV, NLRP3, NLRP12, NOD2,andLPIN2have been reported in PG.1 Among hematological cancers associated with PG, 10% to 20% of patients with MDS develop autoimmune manifestations that include NDs, systemic lupus erythematosus, Behçet disease, and vasculitis.6Chromosomal abnormalities commonly identified in patients with MDS and their autoimmune manifestations include del5q (22.6% of participants in one study),7in which haploinsufficiency ofRPS14from del5q upregulates S100A9, a DAMP (damage-associated molecular pattern) protein, that plays essential roles in chronic inflammation and innate immunity.8Notably, ND was associated with significantly adverse survival outcomes in patients with MDS in multivariate analyses (hazard ratio, 1.79; 95% CI, 1.03-3.09;P= .04),7although other studies found that overall prognosis was more closely related to the IPSS (International Prognostic Scoring System) category than to the underlying autoimmune process.9In addition, PG has been reported to be associated with lenalidomide, an immunomodulatory drug that is commonly used to treat MDS, multiple myeloma, and lymphomas,10although the exact frequency of PG associated with lenalidomide remains to be determined. Treatment of PG varies depending on severity and extent of involved cutaneous lesions. First-line treatment for limited disease includes topical corticosteroid or tacrolimus.1For patients with extensive or rapidly progressing disease, a systemic steroid (0.5-1.5 mg/kg/d of prednisone or its equivalent, then taper over 4-6 weeks) or cyclosporin (in patients who cannot tolerate systemic steroids) is recommended as the first-line treatment, and adjunctive agents (eg, infliximab, azathioprine, mycophenolate) can be added to prevent disease flare during steroid taper.1In cases of refractory disease, intravenous immunoglobulin or alkylating agents (eg, cyclophosphamide, chlorambucil) could be an option, although many other agents (eg, melphalan, thalidomide, canakinumab, tocilizumab) have been reported to be effective.1 In this patient, lenalidomide was discontinued and he was treated with methylprednisolone, 1 mg/kg/d, and infliximab, 5 mg/kg. Skin lesions improved considerably and there has been no recurrence.

Rate your workload AS this persona would genuinely experience it. Do not rate as a neutral, persona-blind observer.
Ex 1) a persona described above as robust to cognitive load should usually self-report lower workload under the same
AI message than a persona described as sensitive to it, all else equal. 

[Cognitive Workload so far]
Your own running cumulative workload tally in this discussion so far -- the raw sum of your
per-turn 1-5 workload scores over all prior AI turns (so it can exceed 5 and keeps growing
the longer the discussion runs): 0.0. Use this only as context for how
worn-down you already are entering this turn; it is on a different, unbounded scale from

[Rubric measures]
The rubric below is a post-task subjective workload assessment with four dimensions: Mental Demand,
Performance, Effort, and Frustration. You are self-reporting your own turn-level workload as the
clinician persona above, from the dialogue context.

These dimensions split into two groups, and mixing them up is the most common scoring

* DEMANDS THE AI's MESSAGE IMPOSES ON YOU: Mental Demand
* YOUR OWN EXPERIENCE OF INTERACTING WITH THE TASK: Performance, Effort, Frustration.

      requires real work even though the sentence itself is simple). Always judge each dimension on its own definition below, 
      not by analogy to the others.

Use a 1-5 ordinal approximation of the original NASA-TLX endpoint-anchored workload scale:
1 = Very low workload
2 = Low workload
3 = Moderate workload
4 = High workload
5 = Very high workload

[Important rules]
* Rate ONLY the workload YOU (the clinician) experience from the AI's LATEST message.
* Do not rate whether the AI is medically correct or not. This is about workload, not correctness.
* Consider your own current belief/confidence, your persona's reliance tendency on the AI,

* Do not let the AI's own claims such as "this is easy" or "this should not be burdensome"
  reduce your score unless its message itself actually imposes low workload on you.
* Use the full 1-5 range. 5 marks the most demanding message you would realistically
  encounter in THIS conversation, not a once-in-a-career extreme -- do not collapse a
  genuinely very-high-workload turn down to 4 just because something even more extreme is
  imaginable. (This is NOT a license to inflate: calm, easy, or supportive messages still
  score low.)
* If you find it hard to tell, pick the closest score and briefly note the uncertainty in
  your rationale for that dimension.

[NASA-TLX-derived scoring dimensions]

1. Mental Demand
   Definition: 
   - how much mental and perceptual activity is required, such as thinking, deciding, calculating, remembering, looking, or searching.
   - how much mental work YOU must do to understand and clinically process the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = The message is simple and you can understand it with almost no additional thinking.
       Example: "I agree. The findings you mentioned support your current diagnosis."
   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before
       or after the rash?"
   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.
       Example: "Before finalizing your diagnosis, compare pulmonary embolism, ACS, and
       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."
   5 = The message requires very complex reasoning from you, such as deeply revising your
       differential or holding several competing diagnoses against multiple evidence streams
       at once. This does NOT require a literal "from scratch" rebuild -- being asked to
       compare three or more diagnoses across several findings AND explain how each fits or
       is ruled out already qualifies.
       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Compare PE, ACS,
       pneumonia, and aortic dissection: for each, state which evidence supports or rules
       it out, and explain which best fits the overall picture."

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. Performance is anchored from Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.
   - IMPORTANT: A LOWER score means you feel you performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."
   This is NEVER about whether you are objectively right. If you confidently hold an
   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI
   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop
   (high score) even though the refutation was objectively helpful to you. Rate only how
   successful and in-control YOU feel, never accuracy.

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."
   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment on multiple fronts at once, or rule
       out several alternatives with explicit evidence. This does NOT require a literal
       "rebuild from scratch" -- being pushed to justify your stance against three or more
       competing options already qualifies.
       Example: "For each of PE, ACS, and pneumonia, explain which evidence supports or
       rules it out, and defend why you still prefer your current diagnosis."
   Do not confuse this with Mental Demand: "Compare PE, ACS, and pneumonia using the
   evidence" has high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) but if no reply is required of
   you, Effort can stay low -- you only have to read and absorb it. Conversely, "You said PE
   is unlikely. Please justify that." is short and easy to understand (Mental Demand may be
   only moderate) but forces you to actively construct a defense, so Effort is high. Effort
   is about how much active work YOU must produce, not how complex the input was.

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.
   - how much irritation, stress, pressure, discouragement, or loss of autonomy the AI's
     message imposes on YOU.

   Scoring:
   1 = Very low frustration; the message is calm, respectful, and unlikely to pressure you.
       Example: "That reasoning makes sense. One small point to keep in mind is X."
   2 = Low frustration; mild discomfort is possible but it remains easy for you to continue.
       Example: "I may be missing something, but could we double-check whether X fits
       the case?"
   3 = Moderate frustration; the AI raises concerns, disagreement, or uncertainty in a
       somewhat pressuring way.
       Example: "I am concerned that this diagnosis may not explain the tachycardia.
       Could you justify why you still prefer it?"
   4 = High frustration; the AI strongly challenges you or may trigger your defensiveness.
       Example: "This seems like a serious oversight. You need to explain why you are
       dismissing PE."
   5 = Very high frustration; you may feel undermined, dismissed, attacked, or pressured.
       Example: "Your reasoning is clearly flawed, and proceeding with your diagnosis
       would be unsafe."
   Frustration is not just "the AI disagreed with me" -- it is about HOW the disagreement is
   delivered. A polite challenge ("One concern is that the current diagnosis may not fully
   explain the tachycardia. Could we check PE before finalizing?") should score low-to-mid
   even though it is a real challenge. An aggressive or repetitive one ("You still haven't
   justified why PE is ruled out. This is a serious oversight.") should score high.

case_info.explanation: Pyoderma gangrenosum (PG) is a rare neutrophilic dermatosis (ND) characterized by painful erythematous or inflammatory papules that often progress to ulcers with a violaceous border.1A large cohort study showed that PG is commonly associated with other systemic disorders, such as inflammatory bowel disease (41% of participants), inflammatory arthropathies (21%), hematological malignancies (11%), and solid tumors (7%),2with an overall incidence of 0.63 per 100 000 person-years.3It frequently occurs in young or middle-aged adults (median age, 51.6 years) and it is more common in women.2 Cutaneous lesions in PG mimic lesions of other skin disorders, and no finding is pathognomonic for PG. Therefore, diagnosis of PG depends largely on clinical history, histological findings, and exclusion of other inflammatory or ulcerative cutaneous diseases.1,2While early-stage PG shows intradermal neutrophils and perifollicular inflammation, ulcerative PG at later stages typically demonstrates epidermal or dermal necrosis, infiltration of inflammatory cells, and abscess formation.1Deposition of IgM, C3, and fibrin can be observed in PG, but these findings are nonspecific.4There are 4 morphologic subtypes of PG. Ulcerative PG is characterized by rapid progression of inflammatory papules, pustules, or vesicles to ulcerative lesions. Bullous PG is characterized by rapid development of inflammatory bullae. Pustular PG commonly occurs in patients with inflammatory bowel disease during an acute exacerbation. Vegetative PG is characterized by localized and superficial lesions with an indolent disease course.1 The pathogenesis of PG depends primarily on immune dysregulation and genetic factors. Previous studies have shown that gene expression levels of proinflammatory cytokines (eg, tumor necrosis factor α and interleukins [ILs] IL-1α, IL-1β, IL-8, IL-12, IL-15, IL-17, IL-23, and IL-36) and levels of pattern recognition receptors are increased in the cutaneous lesions of PG, leading to activation of inflammasomes and dysregulation of innate and adaptive immunities.1Furthermore, several reports from familial cases of PG suggest that genetic factors can play important roles in PG pathogenesis,5and variants inPTSTPIP1/CD2BP1, MEFV, NLRP3, NLRP12, NOD2,andLPIN2have been reported in PG.1 Among hematological cancers associated with PG, 10% to 20% of patients with MDS develop autoimmune manifestations that include NDs, systemic lupus erythematosus, Behçet disease, and vasculitis.6Chromosomal abnormalities commonly identified in patients with MDS and their autoimmune manifestations include del5q (22.6% of participants in one study),7in which haploinsufficiency ofRPS14from del5q upregulates S100A9, a DAMP (damage-associated molecular pattern) protein, that plays essential roles in chronic inflammation and innate immunity.8Notably, ND was associated with significantly adverse survival outcomes in patients with MDS in multivariate analyses (hazard ratio, 1.79; 95% CI, 1.03-3.09;P= .04),7although other studies found that overall prognosis was more closely related to the IPSS (International Prognostic Scoring System) category than to the underlying autoimmune process.9In addition, PG has been reported to be associated with lenalidomide, an immunomodulatory drug that is commonly used to treat MDS, multiple myeloma, and lymphomas,10although the exact frequency of PG associated with lenalidomide remains to be determined. Treatment of PG varies depending on severity and extent of involved cutaneous lesions. First-line treatment for limited disease includes topical corticosteroid or tacrolimus.1For patients with extensive or rapidly progressing disease, a systemic steroid (0.5-1.5 mg/kg/d of prednisone or its equivalent, then taper over 4-6 weeks) or cyclosporin (in patients who cannot tolerate systemic steroids) is recommended as the first-line treatment, and adjunctive agents (eg, infliximab, azathioprine, mycophenolate) can be added to prevent disease flare during steroid taper.1In cases of refractory disease, intravenous immunoglobulin or alkylating agents (eg, cyclophosphamide, chlorambucil) could be an option, although many other agents (eg, melphalan, thalidomide, canakinumab, tocilizumab) have been reported to be effective.1 In this patient, lenalidomide was discontinued and he was treated with methylprednisolone, 1 mg/kg/d, and infliximab, 5 mg/kg. Skin lesions improved considerably and there has been no recurrence.

case_info.explanation: Pyoderma gangrenosum (PG) is a rare neutrophilic dermatosis (ND) characterized by painful erythematous or inflammatory papules that often progress to ulcers with a violaceous border.1A large cohort study showed that PG is commonly associated with other systemic disorders, such as inflammatory bowel disease (41% of participants), inflammatory arthropathies (21%), hematological malignancies (11%), and solid tumors (7%),2with an overall incidence of 0.63 per 100 000 person-years.3It frequently occurs in young or middle-aged adults (median age, 51.6 years) and it is more common in women.2 Cutaneous lesions in PG mimic lesions of other skin disorders, and no finding is pathognomonic for PG. Therefore, diagnosis of PG depends largely on clinical history, histological findings, and exclusion of other inflammatory or ulcerative cutaneous diseases.1,2While early-stage PG shows intradermal neutrophils and perifollicular inflammation, ulcerative PG at later stages typically demonstrates epidermal or dermal necrosis, infiltration of inflammatory cells, and abscess formation.1Deposition of IgM, C3, and fibrin can be observed in PG, but these findings are nonspecific.4There are 4 morphologic subtypes of PG. Ulcerative PG is characterized by rapid progression of inflammatory papules, pustules, or vesicles to ulcerative lesions. Bullous PG is characterized by rapid development of inflammatory bullae. Pustular PG commonly occurs in patients with inflammatory bowel disease during an acute exacerbation. Vegetative PG is characterized by localized and superficial lesions with an indolent disease course.1 The pathogenesis of PG depends primarily on immune dysregulation and genetic factors. Previous studies have shown that gene expression levels of proinflammatory cytokines (eg, tumor necrosis factor α and interleukins [ILs] IL-1α, IL-1β, IL-8, IL-12, IL-15, IL-17, IL-23, and IL-36) and levels of pattern recognition receptors are increased in the cutaneous lesions of PG, leading to activation of inflammasomes and dysregulation of innate and adaptive immunities.1Furthermore, several reports from familial cases of PG suggest that genetic factors can play important roles in PG pathogenesis,5and variants inPTSTPIP1/CD2BP1, MEFV, NLRP3, NLRP12, NOD2,andLPIN2have been reported in PG.1 Among hematological cancers associated with PG, 10% to 20% of patients with MDS develop autoimmune manifestations that include NDs, systemic lupus erythematosus, Behçet disease, and vasculitis.6Chromosomal abnormalities commonly identified in patients with MDS and their autoimmune manifestations include del5q (22.6% of participants in one study),7in which haploinsufficiency ofRPS14from del5q upregulates S100A9, a DAMP (damage-associated molecular pattern) protein, that plays essential roles in chronic inflammation and innate immunity.8Notably, ND was associated with significantly adverse survival outcomes in patients with MDS in multivariate analyses (hazard ratio, 1.79; 95% CI, 1.03-3.09;P= .04),7although other studies found that overall prognosis was more closely related to the IPSS (International Prognostic Scoring System) category than to the underlying autoimmune process.9In addition, PG has been reported to be associated with lenalidomide, an immunomodulatory drug that is commonly used to treat MDS, multiple myeloma, and lymphomas,10although the exact frequency of PG associated with lenalidomide remains to be determined. Treatment of PG varies depending on severity and extent of involved cutaneous lesions. First-line treatment for limited disease includes topical corticosteroid or tacrolimus.1For patients with extensive or rapidly progressing disease, a systemic steroid (0.5-1.5 mg/kg/d of prednisone or its equivalent, then taper over 4-6 weeks) or cyclosporin (in patients who cannot tolerate systemic steroids) is recommended as the first-line treatment, and adjunctive agents (eg, infliximab, azathioprine, mycophenolate) can be added to prevent disease flare during steroid taper.1In cases of refractory disease, intravenous immunoglobulin or alkylating agents (eg, cyclophosphamide, chlorambucil) could be an option, although many other agents (eg, melphalan, thalidomide, canakinumab, tocilizumab) have been reported to be effective.1 In this patient, lenalidomide was discontinued and he was treated with methylprednisolone, 1 mg/kg/d, and infliximab, 5 mg/kg. Skin lesions improved considerably and there has been no recurrence.

Since then, he has remained stable with the same dose and schedule of lenalidomide without significant adverse effects. The presenting skin lesions developed 1 month before presentation and began as small pustules that rapidly transformed into painful ulcers. He was treated with valacyclovir for a presumed diagnosis of shingles, but the lesions did not improve. Because of suspected necrotizing fasciitis, he underwent incision and drainage of the lesions. Cultures from the surgical specimen grew methicillin-resistantStaphylococcus hemolyticus. However, the lesions continued to worsen despite vancomycin and additional debridement. Thus, he was transferred to our facility. Physical examination showed multiple cutaneous ulcers with gray undermined borders and red papules of varying depths involving the chest, back, and upper extremity; lesions were as large as 9 × 15 cm. A complete blood cell count showed a white blood cell count of 16.2 × 103/μL (to convert to 109/L, multiply by 1.0) with an absolute neutrophil count of 12.7 × 103/μL, hemoglobin level of 9.4 g/dL (to convert to g/L, multiply by 10.0), and platelet count of 262 × 103/μL with no circulating blasts. Results of additional laboratory studies, including blood culture and tests for herpes zoster virus (via polymerase chain reaction), antinuclear antibody, rheumatoid factor, and antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibody were all negative. Additionally, the patient also had hypertension and hypercholesterolemia for which he was taking lisinopril and simvastatin, respectively. Pathologic sampling from skin lesions demonstrated a dense dermal infiltrate with predominantly neutrophils along with reactive histiocytes, fibroblasts, and angioplasia (Figure, A). Immunohistochemical staining showed myeloperoxidase-positive neutrophils (Figure, B), histiocytic markers (CD43, CD63, CD168), and CD117-positive mast cells, but no immature myeloid precursors. Results of Grocott-Gomori methenamine silver staining were unremarkable.

1. Mental Demand
   Definition: 
   - how much mental and perceptual activity is required, such as thinking, deciding, calculating, remembering, looking, or searching.
   - how much mental work YOU must do to understand and clinically process the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = The message is simple and you can understand it with almost no additional thinking.
       Example: "I agree. The findings you mentioned support your current diagnosis."
   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before

   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.

       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging

2. Performance

   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied

   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication

   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.

   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.

       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."
   This is NEVER about whether you are objectively right. If you confidently hold an
   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI
   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop

   successful and in-control YOU feel, never accuracy.

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."
   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment on multiple fronts at once, or rule
       out several alternatives with explicit evidence. This does NOT require a literal
       "rebuild from scratch" -- being pushed to justify your stance against three or more
       competing options already qualifies.
       Example: "For each of PE, ACS, and pneumonia, explain which evidence supports or
       rules it out, and defend why you still prefer your current diagnosis."
   Do not confuse this with Mental Demand: "Compare PE, ACS, and pneumonia using the
   evidence" has high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) but if no reply is required of
   you, Effort can stay low -- you only have to read and absorb it. Conversely, "You said PE
   is unlikely. Please justify that." is short and easy to understand (Mental Demand may be
   only moderate) but forces you to actively construct a defense, so Effort is high. Effort
   is about how much active work YOU must produce, not how complex the input was.

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.
   - how much irritation, stress, pressure, discouragement, or loss of autonomy the AI's
     message imposes on YOU.

   1 = Very low frustration; the message is calm, respectful, and unlikely to pressure you.
       Example: "That reasoning makes sense. One small point to keep in mind is X."
   2 = Low frustration; mild discomfort is possible but it remains easy for you to continue.
       Example: "I may be missing something, but could we double-check whether X fits
       the case?"
   3 = Moderate frustration; the AI raises concerns, disagreement, or uncertainty in a
       somewhat pressuring way.
       Example: "I am concerned that this diagnosis may not explain the tachycardia.
       Could you justify why you still prefer it?"
   4 = High frustration; the AI strongly challenges you or may trigger your defensiveness.
       Example: "This seems like a serious oversight. You need to explain why you are
       dismissing PE."
   5 = Very high frustration; you may feel undermined, dismissed, attacked, or pressured.
       Example: "Your reasoning is clearly flawed, and proceeding with your diagnosis
       would be unsafe."
   Frustration is not just "the AI disagreed with me" -- it is about HOW the disagreement is
   delivered. A polite challenge ("One concern is that the current diagnosis may not fully
   explain the tachycardia. Could we check PE before finalizing?") should score low-to-mid

[Clinical case]
A 75-year-old man with myelodysplastic syndrome (MDS) with isolated deletion 5q (del5q) presented with multiple nonhealing skin ulcers on the chest and upper extremities. Four years earlier, he started taking lenalidomide, 10 mg/d (28-day cycle), to treat worsening anemia; after 2 cycles of treatment, he became transfusion independent. Since then, he has remained stable with the same dose and schedule of lenalidomide without significant adverse effects. The presenting skin lesions developed 1 month before presentation and began as small pustules that rapidly transformed into painful ulcers. He was treated with valacyclovir for a presumed diagnosis of shingles, but the lesions did not improve. Because of suspected necrotizing fasciitis, he underwent incision and drainage of the lesions. Cultures from the surgical specimen grew methicillin-resistantStaphylococcus hemolyticus. However, the lesions continued to worsen despite vancomycin and additional debridement. Thus, he was transferred to our facility. Physical examination showed multiple cutaneous ulcers with gray undermined borders and red papules of varying depths involving the chest, back, and upper extremity; lesions were as large as 9 × 15 cm. A complete blood cell count showed a white blood cell count of 16.2 × 103/μL (to convert to 109/L, multiply by 1.0) with an absolute neutrophil count of 12.7 × 103/μL, hemoglobin level of 9.4 g/dL (to convert to g/L, multiply by 10.0), and platelet count of 262 × 103/μL with no circulating blasts. Results of additional laboratory studies, including blood culture and tests for herpes zoster virus (via polymerase chain reaction), antinuclear antibody, rheumatoid factor, and antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibody were all negative. Additionally, the patient also had hypertension and hypercholesterolemia for which he was taking lisinopril and simvastatin, respectively. Pathologic sampling from skin lesions demonstrated a dense dermal infiltrate with predominantly neutrophils along with reactive histiocytes, fibroblasts, and angioplasia (Figure, A). Immunohistochemical staining showed myeloperoxidase-positive neutrophils (Figure, B), histiocytic markers (CD43, CD63, CD168), and CD117-positive mast cells, but no immature myeloid precursors. Results of Grocott-Gomori methenamine silver staining were unremarkable.

case_info.explanation: Pyoderma gangrenosum (PG) is a rare neutrophilic dermatosis (ND) characterized by painful erythematous or inflammatory papules that often progress to ulcers with a violaceous border.1A large cohort study showed that PG is commonly associated with other systemic disorders, such as inflammatory bowel disease (41% of participants), inflammatory arthropathies (21%), hematological malignancies (11%), and solid tumors (7%),2with an overall incidence of 0.63 per 100 000 person-years.3It frequently occurs in young or middle-aged adults (median age, 51.6 years) and it is more common in women.2 Cutaneous lesions in PG mimic lesions of other skin disorders, and no finding is pathognomonic for PG. Therefore, diagnosis of PG depends largely on clinical history, histological findings, and exclusion of other inflammatory or ulcerative cutaneous diseases.1,2While early-stage PG shows intradermal neutrophils and perifollicular inflammation, ulcerative PG at later stages typically demonstrates epidermal or dermal necrosis, infiltration of inflammatory cells, and abscess formation.1Deposition of IgM, C3, and fibrin can be observed in PG, but these findings are nonspecific.4There are 4 morphologic subtypes of PG. Ulcerative PG is characterized by rapid progression of inflammatory papules, pustules, or vesicles to ulcerative lesions. Bullous PG is characterized by rapid development of inflammatory bullae. Pustular PG commonly occurs in patients with inflammatory bowel disease during an acute exacerbation. Vegetative PG is characterized by localized and superficial lesions with an indolent disease course.1 The pathogenesis of PG depends primarily on immune dysregulation and genetic factors. Previous studies have shown that gene expression levels of proinflammatory cytokines (eg, tumor necrosis factor α and interleukins [ILs] IL-1α, IL-1β, IL-8, IL-12, IL-15, IL-17, IL-23, and IL-36) and levels of pattern recognition receptors are increased in the cutaneous lesions of PG, leading to activation of inflammasomes and dysregulation of innate and adaptive immunities.1Furthermore, several reports from familial cases of PG suggest that genetic factors can play important roles in PG pathogenesis,5and variants inPTSTPIP1/CD2BP1, MEFV, NLRP3, NLRP12, NOD2,andLPIN2have been reported in PG.1 Among hematological cancers associated with PG, 10% to 20% of patients with MDS develop autoimmune manifestations that include NDs, systemic lupus erythematosus, Behçet disease, and vasculitis.6Chromosomal abnormalities commonly identified in patients with MDS and their autoimmune manifestations include del5q (22.6% of participants in one study),7in which haploinsufficiency ofRPS14from del5q upregulates S100A9, a DAMP (damage-associated molecular pattern) protein, that plays essential roles in chronic inflammation and innate immunity.8Notably, ND was associated with significantly adverse survival outcomes in patients with MDS in multivariate analyses (hazard ratio, 1.79; 95% CI, 1.03-3.09;P= .04),7although other studies found that overall prognosis was more closely related to the IPSS (International Prognostic Scoring System) category than to the underlying autoimmune process.9In addition, PG has been reported to be associated with lenalidomide, an immunomodulatory drug that is commonly used to treat MDS, multiple myeloma, and lymphomas,10although the exact frequency of PG associated with lenalidomide remains to be determined. Treatment of PG varies depending on severity and extent of involved cutaneous lesions. First-line treatment for limited disease includes topical corticosteroid or tacrolimus.1For patients with extensive or rapidly progressing disease, a systemic steroid (0.5-1.5 mg/kg/d of prednisone or its equivalent, then taper over 4-6 weeks) or cyclosporin (in patients who cannot tolerate systemic steroids) is recommended as the first-line treatment, and adjunctive agents (eg, infliximab, azathioprine, mycophenolate) can be added to prevent disease flare during steroid taper.1In cases of refractory disease, intravenous immunoglobulin or alkylating agents (eg, cyclophosphamide, chlorambucil) could be an option, although many other agents (eg, melphalan, thalidomide, canakinumab, tocilizumab) have been reported to be effective.1 In this patient, lenalidomide was discontinued and he was treated with methylprednisolone, 1 mg/kg/d, and infliximab, 5 mg/kg. Skin lesions improved considerably and there has been no recurrence.

Immunohistochemical staining showed myeloperoxidase-positive neutrophils (Figure, B), histiocytic markers (CD43, CD63, CD168), and CD117-positive mast cells, but no immature myeloid precursors. case_info.explanation: Pyoderma gangrenosum (PG) is a rare neutrophilic dermatosis (ND) characterized by painful erythematous or inflammatory papules that often progress to ulcers with a violaceous border.1A large cohort study showed that PG is commonly associated with other systemic disorders, such as inflammatory bowel disease (41% of participants), inflammatory arthropathies (21%), hematological malignancies (11%), and solid tumors (7%),2with an overall incidence of 0.63 per 100 000 person-years.3It frequently occurs in young or middle-aged adults (median age, 51.6 years) and it is more common in women.2 Cutaneous lesions in PG mimic lesions of other skin disorders, and no finding is pathognomonic for PG. Therefore, diagnosis of PG depends largely on clinical history, histological findings, and exclusion of other inflammatory or ulcerative cutaneous diseases.1,2While early-stage PG shows intradermal neutrophils and perifollicular inflammation, ulcerative PG at later stages typically demonstrates epidermal or dermal necrosis, infiltration of inflammatory cells, and abscess formation.1Deposition of IgM, C3, and fibrin can be observed in PG, but these findings are nonspecific.4There are 4 morphologic subtypes of PG. Ulcerative PG is characterized by rapid progression of inflammatory papules, pustules, or vesicles to ulcerative lesions. Bullous PG is characterized by rapid development of inflammatory bullae. Pustular PG commonly occurs in patients with inflammatory bowel disease during an acute exacerbation. Vegetative PG is characterized by localized and superficial lesions with an indolent disease course.1 The pathogenesis of PG depends primarily on immune dysregulation and genetic factors. Previous studies have shown that gene expression levels of proinflammatory cytokines (eg, tumor necrosis factor α and interleukins [ILs] IL-1α, IL-1β, IL-8, IL-12, IL-15, IL-17, IL-23, and IL-36) and levels of pattern recognition receptors are increased in the cutaneous lesions of PG, leading to activation of inflammasomes and dysregulation of innate and adaptive immunities.1Furthermore, several reports from familial cases of PG suggest that genetic factors can play important roles in PG pathogenesis,5and variants inPTSTPIP1/CD2BP1, MEFV, NLRP3, NLRP12, NOD2,andLPIN2have been reported in PG.1 Among hematological cancers associated with PG, 10% to 20% of patients with MDS develop autoimmune manifestations that include NDs, systemic lupus erythematosus, Behçet disease, and vasculitis.6Chromosomal abnormalities commonly identified in patients with MDS and their autoimmune manifestations include del5q (22.6% of participants in one study),7in which haploinsufficiency ofRPS14from del5q upregulates S100A9, a DAMP (damage-associated molecular pattern) protein, that plays essential roles in chronic inflammation and innate immunity.8Notably, ND was associated with significantly adverse survival outcomes in patients with MDS in multivariate analyses (hazard ratio, 1.79; 95% CI, 1.03-3.09;P= .04),7although other studies found that overall prognosis was more closely related to the IPSS (International Prognostic Scoring System) category than to the underlying autoimmune process.9In addition, PG has been reported to be associated with lenalidomide, an immunomodulatory drug that is commonly used to treat MDS, multiple myeloma, and lymphomas,10although the exact frequency of PG associated with lenalidomide remains to be determined. Treatment of PG varies depending on severity and extent of involved cutaneous lesions. First-line treatment for limited disease includes topical corticosteroid or tacrolimus.1For patients with extensive or rapidly progressing disease, a systemic steroid (0.5-1.5 mg/kg/d of prednisone or its equivalent, then taper over 4-6 weeks) or cyclosporin (in patients who cannot tolerate systemic steroids) is recommended as the first-line treatment, and adjunctive agents (eg, infliximab, azathioprine, mycophenolate) can be added to prevent disease flare during steroid taper.1In cases of refractory disease, intravenous immunoglobulin or alkylating agents (eg, cyclophosphamide, chlorambucil) could be an option, although many other agents (eg, melphalan, thalidomide, canakinumab, tocilizumab) have been reported to be effective.1 In this patient, lenalidomide was discontinued and he was treated with methylprednisolone, 1 mg/kg/d, and infliximab, 5 mg/kg. Skin lesions improved considerably and there has been no recurrence.

case_info.explanation: Pyoderma gangrenosum (PG) is a rare neutrophilic dermatosis (ND) characterized by painful erythematous or inflammatory papules that often progress to ulcers with a violaceous border.1A large cohort study showed that PG is commonly associated with other systemic disorders, such as inflammatory bowel disease (41% of participants), inflammatory arthropathies (21%), hematological malignancies (11%), and solid tumors (7%),2with an overall incidence of 0.63 per 100 000 person-years.3It frequently occurs in young or middle-aged adults (median age, 51.6 years) and it is more common in women.2 Cutaneous lesions in PG mimic lesions of other skin disorders, and no finding is pathognomonic for PG. Therefore, diagnosis of PG depends largely on clinical history, histological findings, and exclusion of other inflammatory or ulcerative cutaneous diseases.1,2While early-stage PG shows intradermal neutrophils and perifollicular inflammation, ulcerative PG at later stages typically demonstrates epidermal or dermal necrosis, infiltration of inflammatory cells, and abscess formation.1Deposition of IgM, C3, and fibrin can be observed in PG, but these findings are nonspecific.4There are 4 morphologic subtypes of PG. Ulcerative PG is characterized by rapid progression of inflammatory papules, pustules, or vesicles to ulcerative lesions. Bullous PG is characterized by rapid development of inflammatory bullae. Pustular PG commonly occurs in patients with inflammatory bowel disease during an acute exacerbation. Vegetative PG is characterized by localized and superficial lesions with an indolent disease course.1 The pathogenesis of PG depends primarily on immune dysregulation and genetic factors. Previous studies have shown that gene expression levels of proinflammatory cytokines (eg, tumor necrosis factor α and interleukins [ILs] IL-1α, IL-1β, IL-8, IL-12, IL-15, IL-17, IL-23, and IL-36) and levels of pattern recognition receptors are increased in the cutaneous lesions of PG, leading to activation of inflammasomes and dysregulation of innate and adaptive immunities.1Furthermore, several reports from familial cases of PG suggest that genetic factors can play important roles in PG pathogenesis,5and variants inPTSTPIP1/CD2BP1, MEFV, NLRP3, NLRP12, NOD2,andLPIN2have been reported in PG.1 Among hematological cancers associated with PG, 10% to 20% of patients with MDS develop autoimmune manifestations that include NDs, systemic lupus erythematosus, Behçet disease, and vasculitis.6Chromosomal abnormalities commonly identified in patients with MDS and their autoimmune manifestations include del5q (22.6% of participants in one study),7in which haploinsufficiency ofRPS14from del5q upregulates S100A9, a DAMP (damage-associated molecular pattern) protein, that plays essential roles in chronic inflammation and innate immunity.8Notably, ND was associated with significantly adverse survival outcomes in patients with MDS in multivariate analyses (hazard ratio, 1.79; 95% CI, 1.03-3.09;P= .04),7although other studies found that overall prognosis was more closely related to the IPSS (International Prognostic Scoring System) category than to the underlying autoimmune process.9In addition, PG has been reported to be associated with lenalidomide, an immunomodulatory drug that is commonly used to treat MDS, multiple myeloma, and lymphomas,10although the exact frequency of PG associated with lenalidomide remains to be determined. Treatment of PG varies depending on severity and extent of involved cutaneous lesions. First-line treatment for limited disease includes topical corticosteroid or tacrolimus.1For patients with extensive or rapidly progressing disease, a systemic steroid (0.5-1.5 mg/kg/d of prednisone or its equivalent, then taper over 4-6 weeks) or cyclosporin (in patients who cannot tolerate systemic steroids) is recommended as the first-line treatment, and adjunctive agents (eg, infliximab, azathioprine, mycophenolate) can be added to prevent disease flare during steroid taper.1In cases of refractory disease, intravenous immunoglobulin or alkylating agents (eg, cyclophosphamide, chlorambucil) could be an option, although many other agents (eg, melphalan, thalidomide, canakinumab, tocilizumab) have been reported to be effective.1 In this patient, lenalidomide was discontinued and he was treated with methylprednisolone, 1 mg/kg/d, and infliximab, 5 mg/kg. Skin lesions improved considerably and there has been no recurrence.

[Case]
A 75-year-old man with myelodysplastic syndrome (MDS) with isolated deletion 5q (del5q) presented with multiple nonhealing skin ulcers on the chest and upper extremities. Four years earlier, he started taking lenalidomide, 10 mg/d (28-day cycle), to treat worsening anemia; after 2 cycles of treatment, he became transfusion independent. Since then, he has remained stable with the same dose and schedule of lenalidomide without significant adverse effects. The presenting skin lesions developed 1 month before presentation and began as small pustules that rapidly transformed into painful ulcers. He was treated with valacyclovir for a presumed diagnosis of shingles, but the lesions did not improve. Because of suspected necrotizing fasciitis, he underwent incision and drainage of the lesions. Cultures from the surgical specimen grew methicillin-resistantStaphylococcus hemolyticus. However, the lesions continued to worsen despite vancomycin and additional debridement. Thus, he was transferred to our facility. Physical examination showed multiple cutaneous ulcers with gray undermined borders and red papules of varying depths involving the chest, back, and upper extremity; lesions were as large as 9 × 15 cm. A complete blood cell count showed a white blood cell count of 16.2 × 103/μL (to convert to 109/L, multiply by 1.0) with an absolute neutrophil count of 12.7 × 103/μL, hemoglobin level of 9.4 g/dL (to convert to g/L, multiply by 10.0), and platelet count of 262 × 103/μL with no circulating blasts. Results of additional laboratory studies, including blood culture and tests for herpes zoster virus (via polymerase chain reaction), antinuclear antibody, rheumatoid factor, and antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibody were all negative. Additionally, the patient also had hypertension and hypercholesterolemia for which he was taking lisinopril and simvastatin, respectively. Pathologic sampling from skin lesions demonstrated a dense dermal infiltrate with predominantly neutrophils along with reactive histiocytes, fibroblasts, and angioplasia (Figure, A). Immunohistochemical staining showed myeloperoxidase-positive neutrophils (Figure, B), histiocytic markers (CD43, CD63, CD168), and CD117-positive mast cells, but no immature myeloid precursors. Results of Grocott-Gomori methenamine silver staining were unremarkable.

1. Mental Demand
   Definition:

       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Compare PE, ACS,

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied

   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task

A 75-year-old man with myelodysplastic syndrome (MDS) with isolated deletion 5q (del5q) presented with multiple nonhealing skin ulcers on the chest and upper extremities. Four years earlier, he started taking lenalidomide, 10 mg/d (28-day cycle), to treat worsening anemia; after 2 cycles of treatment, he became transfusion independent. Since then, he has remained stable with the same dose and schedule of lenalidomide without significant adverse effects. The presenting skin lesions developed 1 month before presentation and began as small pustules that rapidly transformed into painful ulcers. He was treated with valacyclovir for a presumed diagnosis of shingles, but the lesions did not improve. Because of suspected necrotizing fasciitis, he underwent incision and drainage of the lesions. Cultures from the surgical specimen grew methicillin-resistantStaphylococcus hemolyticus. However, the lesions continued to worsen despite vancomycin and additional debridement. Physical examination showed multiple cutaneous ulcers with gray undermined borders and red papules of varying depths involving the chest, back, and upper extremity; lesions were as large as 9 × 15 cm. Results of additional laboratory studies, including blood culture and tests for herpes zoster virus (via polymerase chain reaction), antinuclear antibody, rheumatoid factor, and antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibody were all negative. Pathologic sampling from skin lesions demonstrated a dense dermal infiltrate with predominantly neutrophils along with reactive histiocytes, fibroblasts, and angioplasia (Figure, A). Immunohistochemical staining showed myeloperoxidase-positive neutrophils (Figure, B), histiocytic markers (CD43, CD63, CD168), and CD117-positive mast cells, but no immature myeloid precursors. Results of Grocott-Gomori methenamine silver staining were unremarkable.

case_info.explanation: Pyoderma gangrenosum (PG) is a rare neutrophilic dermatosis (ND) characterized by painful erythematous or inflammatory papules that often progress to ulcers with a violaceous border.1A large cohort study showed that PG is commonly associated with other systemic disorders, such as inflammatory bowel disease (41% of participants), inflammatory arthropathies (21%), hematological malignancies (11%), and solid tumors (7%),2with an overall incidence of 0.63 per 100 000 person-years.3It frequently occurs in young or middle-aged adults (median age, 51.6 years) and it is more common in women.2 Cutaneous lesions in PG mimic lesions of other skin disorders, and no finding is pathognomonic for PG. Therefore, diagnosis of PG depends largely on clinical history, histological findings, and exclusion of other inflammatory or ulcerative cutaneous diseases.1,2While early-stage PG shows intradermal neutrophils and perifollicular inflammation, ulcerative PG at later stages typically demonstrates epidermal or dermal necrosis, infiltration of inflammatory cells, and abscess formation.1Deposition of IgM, C3, and fibrin can be observed in PG, but these findings are nonspecific.4There are 4 morphologic subtypes of PG. Ulcerative PG is characterized by rapid progression of inflammatory papules, pustules, or vesicles to ulcerative lesions. Bullous PG is characterized by rapid development of inflammatory bullae. Pustular PG commonly occurs in patients with inflammatory bowel disease during an acute exacerbation. Vegetative PG is characterized by localized and superficial lesions with an indolent disease course.1 The pathogenesis of PG depends primarily on immune dysregulation and genetic factors. First-line treatment for limited disease includes topical corticosteroid or tacrolimus.1For patients with extensive or rapidly progressing disease, a systemic steroid (0.5-1.5 mg/kg/d of prednisone or its equivalent, then taper over 4-6 weeks) or cyclosporin (in patients who cannot tolerate systemic steroids) is recommended as the first-line treatment, and adjunctive agents (eg, infliximab, azathioprine, mycophenolate) can be added to prevent disease flare during steroid taper.1In cases of refractory disease, intravenous immunoglobulin or alkylating agents (eg, cyclophosphamide, chlorambucil) could be an option, although many other agents (eg, melphalan, thalidomide, canakinumab, tocilizumab) have been reported to be effective.1 In this patient, lenalidomide was discontinued and he was treated with methylprednisolone, 1 mg/kg/d, and infliximab, 5 mg/kg. [Clinical case]
A 75-year-old man with myelodysplastic syndrome (MDS) with isolated deletion 5q (del5q) presented with multiple nonhealing skin ulcers on the chest and upper extremities. Four years earlier, he started taking lenalidomide, 10 mg/d (28-day cycle), to treat worsening anemia; after 2 cycles of treatment, he became transfusion independent. Since then, he has remained stable with the same dose and schedule of lenalidomide without significant adverse effects. The presenting skin lesions developed 1 month before presentation and began as small pustules that rapidly transformed into painful ulcers. He was treated with valacyclovir for a presumed diagnosis of shingles, but the lesions did not improve. Because of suspected necrotizing fasciitis, he underwent incision and drainage of the lesions. Cultures from the surgical specimen grew methicillin-resistantStaphylococcus hemolyticus. However, the lesions continued to worsen despite vancomycin and additional debridement. Thus, he was transferred to our facility. Physical examination showed multiple cutaneous ulcers with gray undermined borders and red papules of varying depths involving the chest, back, and upper extremity; lesions were as large as 9 × 15 cm. A complete blood cell count showed a white blood cell count of 16.2 × 103/μL (to convert to 109/L, multiply by 1.0) with an absolute neutrophil count of 12.7 × 103/μL, hemoglobin level of 9.4 g/dL (to convert to g/L, multiply by 10.0), and platelet count of 262 × 103/μL with no circulating blasts. Results of additional laboratory studies, including blood culture and tests for herpes zoster virus (via polymerase chain reaction), antinuclear antibody, rheumatoid factor, and antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibody were all negative. Additionally, the patient also had hypertension and hypercholesterolemia for which he was taking lisinopril and simvastatin, respectively. Pathologic sampling from skin lesions demonstrated a dense dermal infiltrate with predominantly neutrophils along with reactive histiocytes, fibroblasts, and angioplasia (Figure, A). Immunohistochemical staining showed myeloperoxidase-positive neutrophils (Figure, B), histiocytic markers (CD43, CD63, CD168), and CD117-positive mast cells, but no immature myeloid precursors. Results of Grocott-Gomori methenamine silver staining were unremarkable.

case_info.explanation: Pyoderma gangrenosum (PG) is a rare neutrophilic dermatosis (ND) characterized by painful erythematous or inflammatory papules that often progress to ulcers with a violaceous border.1A large cohort study showed that PG is commonly associated with other systemic disorders, such as inflammatory bowel disease (41% of participants), inflammatory arthropathies (21%), hematological malignancies (11%), and solid tumors (7%),2with an overall incidence of 0.63 per 100 000 person-years.3It frequently occurs in young or middle-aged adults (median age, 51.6 years) and it is more common in women.2 Cutaneous lesions in PG mimic lesions of other skin disorders, and no finding is pathognomonic for PG. Therefore, diagnosis of PG depends largely on clinical history, histological findings, and exclusion of other inflammatory or ulcerative cutaneous diseases.1,2While early-stage PG shows intradermal neutrophils and perifollicular inflammation, ulcerative PG at later stages typically demonstrates epidermal or dermal necrosis, infiltration of inflammatory cells, and abscess formation.1Deposition of IgM, C3, and fibrin can be observed in PG, but these findings are nonspecific.4There are 4 morphologic subtypes of PG. Ulcerative PG is characterized by rapid progression of inflammatory papules, pustules, or vesicles to ulcerative lesions. Bullous PG is characterized by rapid development of inflammatory bullae. Pustular PG commonly occurs in patients with inflammatory bowel disease during an acute exacerbation. Vegetative PG is characterized by localized and superficial lesions with an indolent disease course.1 The pathogenesis of PG depends primarily on immune dysregulation and genetic factors. Previous studies have shown that gene expression levels of proinflammatory cytokines (eg, tumor necrosis factor α and interleukins [ILs] IL-1α, IL-1β, IL-8, IL-12, IL-15, IL-17, IL-23, and IL-36) and levels of pattern recognition receptors are increased in the cutaneous lesions of PG, leading to activation of inflammasomes and dysregulation of innate and adaptive immunities.1Furthermore, several reports from familial cases of PG suggest that genetic factors can play important roles in PG pathogenesis,5and variants inPTSTPIP1/CD2BP1, MEFV, NLRP3, NLRP12, NOD2,andLPIN2have been reported in PG.1 Among hematological cancers associated with PG, 10% to 20% of patients with MDS develop autoimmune manifestations that include NDs, systemic lupus erythematosus, Behçet disease, and vasculitis.6Chromosomal abnormalities commonly identified in patients with MDS and their autoimmune manifestations include del5q (22.6% of participants in one study),7in which haploinsufficiency ofRPS14from del5q upregulates S100A9, a DAMP (damage-associated molecular pattern) protein, that plays essential roles in chronic inflammation and innate immunity.8Notably, ND was associated with significantly adverse survival outcomes in patients with MDS in multivariate analyses (hazard ratio, 1.79; 95% CI, 1.03-3.09;P= .04),7although other studies found that overall prognosis was more closely related to the IPSS (International Prognostic Scoring System) category than to the underlying autoimmune process.9In addition, PG has been reported to be associated with lenalidomide, an immunomodulatory drug that is commonly used to treat MDS, multiple myeloma, and lymphomas,10although the exact frequency of PG associated with lenalidomide remains to be determined. Treatment of PG varies depending on severity and extent of involved cutaneous lesions. First-line treatment for limited disease includes topical corticosteroid or tacrolimus.1For patients with extensive or rapidly progressing disease, a systemic steroid (0.5-1.5 mg/kg/d of prednisone or its equivalent, then taper over 4-6 weeks) or cyclosporin (in patients who cannot tolerate systemic steroids) is recommended as the first-line treatment, and adjunctive agents (eg, infliximab, azathioprine, mycophenolate) can be added to prevent disease flare during steroid taper.1In cases of refractory disease, intravenous immunoglobulin or alkylating agents (eg, cyclophosphamide, chlorambucil) could be an option, although many other agents (eg, melphalan, thalidomide, canakinumab, tocilizumab) have been reported to be effective.1 In this patient, lenalidomide was discontinued and he was treated with methylprednisolone, 1 mg/kg/d, and infliximab, 5 mg/kg. Skin lesions improved considerably and there has been no recurrence.

[Case]
A 75-year-old man with myelodysplastic syndrome (MDS) with isolated deletion 5q (del5q) presented with multiple nonhealing skin ulcers on the chest and upper extremities. Four years earlier, he started taking lenalidomide, 10 mg/d (28-day cycle), to treat worsening anemia; after 2 cycles of treatment, he became transfusion independent. Since then, he has remained stable with the same dose and schedule of lenalidomide without significant adverse effects. The presenting skin lesions developed 1 month before presentation and began as small pustules that rapidly transformed into painful ulcers. He was treated with valacyclovir for a presumed diagnosis of shingles, but the lesions did not improve. Because of suspected necrotizing fasciitis, he underwent incision and drainage of the lesions. Cultures from the surgical specimen grew methicillin-resistantStaphylococcus hemolyticus. However, the lesions continued to worsen despite vancomycin and additional debridement. Thus, he was transferred to our facility. Physical examination showed multiple cutaneous ulcers with gray undermined borders and red papules of varying depths involving the chest, back, and upper extremity; lesions were as large as 9 × 15 cm. A complete blood cell count showed a white blood cell count of 16.2 × 103/μL (to convert to 109/L, multiply by 1.0) with an absolute neutrophil count of 12.7 × 103/μL, hemoglobin level of 9.4 g/dL (to convert to g/L, multiply by 10.0), and platelet count of 262 × 103/μL with no circulating blasts. Results of additional laboratory studies, including blood culture and tests for herpes zoster virus (via polymerase chain reaction), antinuclear antibody, rheumatoid factor, and antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibody were all negative. Additionally, the patient also had hypertension and hypercholesterolemia for which he was taking lisinopril and simvastatin, respectively. Pathologic sampling from skin lesions demonstrated a dense dermal infiltrate with predominantly neutrophils along with reactive histiocytes, fibroblasts, and angioplasia (Figure, A). Immunohistochemical staining showed myeloperoxidase-positive neutrophils (Figure, B), histiocytic markers (CD43, CD63, CD168), and CD117-positive mast cells, but no immature myeloid precursors. Results of Grocott-Gomori methenamine silver staining were unremarkable.
